MultiFlow 0.2.0 · MIT License
Liu Lab, Yale University

Version 0.2.0 · pip install from GitHub

Generate paired RNA and ATAC cells, and predict how they respond to a perturbation

MultiFlow is a coupled flow-matching model for paired single-cell RNA and ATAC. It does two things. It generates paired profiles of a chosen cell type, and it predicts the response to a perturbation, such as a transcription-factor knockout, in both modalities, including in cell types whose perturbed cells were never seen in training. The two modalities read each other at every integration step.

InstallOne-minute quick startTutorialsOpen the Attention Explorer
Task 1Cell-state generationGenerate paired RNA and ATAC profiles for a named cell type. The tutorial trains on the public OpenProblems multiome data and scores the generated cells against held-out cells. Task 2Perturbation predictionPredict the paired response to a knockout in a held-out cell type. The tutorial repeats the leave-one-cell-type-out benchmark on the GSE274113 Perturb-multiome data. InterpretationAttention ExplorerBrowse the 512 × 512 cross-attention maps of trained models and the peak–gene links they propose.

MIT

Both tasks use the same few functions. Each one reads and writes files and returns the path it wrote:

python
import multiflow as mf

# perturbation prediction for a held-out cell type
ae = mf.train_autoencoder("cells.h5mu", "runs/autoencoder")
encoded = mf.encode("cells.h5mu", "encoded.h5mu", task="perturbation", autoencoder=ae)
fold = mf.prepare_perturbation_fold(encoded, "fold.h5mu", held_out_cell_type="Pro-E")
run = mf.train(fold, "runs/multiflow", model="perturbation",
               perturbation_key="perturbation")
predicted = mf.predict_perturbations(run, "predicted.h5mu", training_fold=fold,
                                     held_out_cell_type="Pro-E", autoencoder=ae,
                                     n_cells=500)
mf.metrics.evaluate_perturbation("cells.h5mu", predicted, cell_type="Pro-E")

Cell-state generation swaps the middle steps for mf.train(encoded, ...), mf.generate and mf.decode; see the quick start.

How the documentation is organised#

  • Installation: one pip command; nothing else to clone.
  • Quick start runs both tasks on a small simulated dataset in about a minute on a CPU. Use it to check an installation.
  • Tutorials reproduce the two benchmarks of the paper from the raw data, as notebooks: cell-state generation and perturbation prediction.
  • User guide explains the data format, the models, training and sampling, and the outputs you get back; the FAQ collects common errors and a glossary.
  • Reference documents every public Python function and class and every command.

Getting started

Installation

MultiFlow is one Python package built on PyTorch. It contains the flow model, the encoders and decoders that take raw profiles to latent states and back, and the metrics of the paper. Nothing else has to be cloned or installed.

shell
pip install "git+https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git"

pip takes the current version from the GitHub repository and builds it; git has to be installed.

python
import multiflow as mf
print(mf.__version__)        # 0.2.0

Names The Python package and the command are both called multiflow. The distribution is called multiflow-omics, because the name multiflow on PyPI belongs to an unrelated project. Do not run pip install multiflow, which installs that other project.

Requirements#

Component Version Notes
Python 3.10 to 3.13 Tested in continuous integration.
PyTorch ≥ 2.1 Installed automatically. If you train on a GPU and need a specific CUDA build, install that PyTorch build first.
anndata, mudata, h5py anndata ≥ 0.9, mudata ≥ 0.2, h5py ≥ 3.8 Read and write paired H5MU files. Installed automatically.
NumPy, pandas, SciPy NumPy ≥ 1.24, pandas ≥ 2.0, SciPy ≥ 1.10 Installed automatically.

The quick start runs on a CPU in about a minute. Training on the datasets of the paper needs a GPU.

Optional extras#

Extra Adds Used for
multiflow-omics[notebooks] matplotlib, scanpy, ipykernel the figures at the end of the tutorial notebooks
multiflow-omics[ilisi] scib, scanpy the scIB iLISI next to the built-in metrics
shell
pip install "multiflow-omics[notebooks] @ git+https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git"

The models, the encoders and the built-in metrics need none of them.

Install from a downloaded file#

The wheel and the source archive are on the Download page; pip installs either directly.

shell
pip install multiflow_omics-0.2.0-py3-none-any.whl
# or
pip install MultiFlow-0.2.0-source.zip

Check the installation#

shell
multiflow --version          # multiflow 0.2.0

Then run the quick start: it trains and evaluates a small model end to end.

Development install#

shell
git clone https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git
cd MultiFlow
pip install -e ".[dev]"
ruff check .
pytest

The test suite covers the models, training, sampling, the autoencoder, both workflows from raw profiles to metrics, checkpoint migration, H5MU validation and the command line. MULTIFLOW_TEST_NOTEBOOKS=1 pytest also executes the two tutorial notebooks in their quick mode.

Getting started

Quick start

Both tasks on a small simulated dataset, from raw profiles to metrics. Everything on this page runs on a laptop CPU in about a minute.

What this example is mf.simulate_h5mu writes 2,400 paired cells of four cell types with three knockouts and a control group, in the same format as real data: raw RNA counts and binary ATAC. The networks below are small so that they train in seconds. For real data, use the default sizes and the settings of the tutorials.

python
import multiflow as mf

data = mf.simulate_h5mu("demo/cells.h5mu")
small = dict(rna_dims=(128, 64, 16), atac_dims=(128, 64, 16))   # paper: the defaults

Perturbation prediction#

Train the autoencoder and encode the cells#

python
autoencoder = mf.train_autoencoder(data, "demo/autoencoder", epochs=40, **small)
encoded = mf.encode(data, "demo/encoded.h5mu", task="perturbation",
                    autoencoder=autoencoder)

MultiFlow works on latent states. The paired autoencoder is trained on the raw profiles, and encode stores the latent state of every cell in the output file.

Hold out one cell type and train#

python
fold = mf.prepare_perturbation_fold(encoded, "demo/fold.h5mu",
                                    held_out_cell_type="type A")
run = mf.train(fold, "demo/multiflow", model="perturbation",
               perturbation_key="perturbation", epochs=15, hidden_dim=64, batch_size=64)

The fold contains every cell except the perturbed cells of type A; its control cells stay. The run folder holds model.pt, run.json and history.csv.

Predict the held-out cells and score them#

python
predicted = mf.predict_perturbations(run, "demo/predicted.h5mu", training_fold=fold,
                                     held_out_cell_type="type A",
                                     autoencoder=autoencoder, n_cells=200)
table = mf.metrics.evaluate_perturbation(data, predicted, cell_type="type A")
print(table[["perturbation", "pcc_delta", "delta_mse", "mmd"]])

predicted.h5mu holds 200 predicted cells per knockout, with RNA as counts drawn from the negative binomial of the autoencoder and ATAC as binary accessibility. pcc_delta is the correlation between the predicted and the observed change of expression on the 100 genes that respond most strongly; on this simulated dataset it is about 0.8.

Cell-state generation#

Split, train the encoders, encode#

python
train, test = mf.split_h5mu(data, "demo/split")
autoencoder = mf.train_autoencoder(train, "demo/gen_autoencoder", epochs=40, **small)
rna_vae = mf.train_rna_vae(train, "demo/rna_vae", max_steps=300)
encoded = mf.encode(train, "demo/train_encoded.h5mu", task="generation",
                    autoencoder=autoencoder, rna_vae=rna_vae)

For generation, RNA goes through a VAE on log-normalised expression and ATAC through the autoencoder. The test cells are set aside before anything is trained.

Train, generate, decode#

python
run = mf.train(encoded, "demo/gen_multiflow", model="cell-state",
               epochs=30, hidden_dim=64, batch_size=64)
latent = mf.generate(run, "demo/generated_latent.h5mu",
                     n={"type A": 100, "type B": 100})
profiles = mf.decode(latent, "demo/generated_profiles.h5mu", task="generation",
                     reference=encoded, autoencoder=autoencoder, rna_vae=rna_vae)

Cell types are given by name; an unknown name is rejected with the list of valid ones.

Compare with the held-out cells#

python
print(mf.metrics.evaluate_generation(test, profiles))

One row per modality: the correlation of the mean profiles (pcc, scc), two MMD estimates and the mixing of real and generated cells among nearest neighbours.

Look at a result#

python
import mudata as md

cells = md.read_h5mu("demo/generated_profiles.h5mu")
print(cells["rna"].shape, cells["atac"].shape)        # (200, 300) (200, 600)
print(cells["rna"].obs["cell_type"].value_counts())

Every output file records how it was made: checkpoint checksums, seeds, integration steps and settings are stored in its uns. See Outputs and reproducibility.

The same on the command line#

Every file-level step is also a command, for example:

shell
multiflow paper train-autoencoder --input demo/cells.h5mu \
  --output-dir demo/autoencoder --epochs 40
multiflow train --input demo/fold.h5mu --output demo/multiflow --model perturbation \
  --perturbation-key perturbation --epochs 15 --hidden-dim 64 --batch-size 64

The command-line reference lists all commands and options.

Tutorial 1 · notebook

Cell-state generation

Train MultiFlow on the OpenProblems bone-marrow multiome data, generate paired RNA and ATAC profiles for all 22 cell types, and score them against held-out cells with the metrics of Fig. 2 of the paper. Everything is trained from scratch with the Python API.

Run it yourself This page is the notebook generation_openproblems.ipynb, also in the tutorials/ folder of the repository. It needs MultiFlow (installation), a GPU and the 8.4 GB dataset, which the notebook downloads. Set QUICK = True in its first cell to run the same steps on a small simulated dataset in about a minute on a CPU. On a Slurm cluster, one command runs it as a job.

Step Function
Download and split the data mf.download_dataset, mf.split_h5mu
Train the two encoders mf.train_autoencoder, mf.train_rna_vae
Encode the training cells mf.encode
Train MultiFlow mf.train
Generate and decode cells mf.generate, mf.decode
Score against held-out cells mf.metrics.evaluate_generation
python
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import multiflow as mf

QUICK = os.environ.get("MULTIFLOW_QUICK") == "1"  # or simply: QUICK = True
DEVICE = None  # None uses the GPU when there is one

if QUICK:  # simulated data and small networks: about a minute on a CPU
    WORK = Path("runs/generation_quick")
    AUTOENCODER = dict(epochs=40, rna_dims=(128, 64, 16), atac_dims=(128, 64, 16))
    RNA_VAE = dict(max_steps=300)
    FLOW = dict(epochs=30, hidden_dim=64, batch_size=64)
else:  # the settings of the paper
    WORK = Path("runs/generation")
    AUTOENCODER = dict(epochs=300)
    RNA_VAE = dict(max_steps=200_000)
    FLOW = dict(epochs=1600)

SCIMILARITY_DIR = Path("external/annotation_model_v1")  # optional, see section 2

started = time.time()
print("multiflow-omics", mf.__version__)
multiflow-omics 0.2.0

1. Data#

The file is 8.4 GB (Figshare, CC BY 4.0). RNA holds raw counts and ATAC is binary. One fifth of the cells of every cell type is set aside; these cells are used only for the metrics in section 5.

python
if QUICK:
    data = WORK / "simulated.h5mu"
    if not data.exists():
        mf.simulate_h5mu(data, n_perturbations=0)
else:
    data = mf.download_dataset(
        "openproblem", "data/openproblem_filtered.h5mu", accept_license=True
    )

report = mf.validate_h5mu(data)
print(f"{report['n_obs']:,} cells, {report['n_conditions']} cell types")
print("raw RNA counts and binary ATAC:", report["paired_raw_contract_ok"])

train, test = WORK / "split" / "train.h5mu", WORK / "split" / "test.h5mu"
if not train.exists():
    mf.split_h5mu(data, WORK / "split", train_fraction=0.8)
69,249 cells, 22 cell types
raw RNA counts and binary ATAC: True

2. Encoders#

MultiFlow models 128-dimensional latent states, not the profiles themselves. For generation, RNA is encoded by a VAE on log-normalised expression and ATAC by the ATAC branch of the paired autoencoder. Both are trained on the training cells only.

In the paper the hidden layers of the RNA VAE start from the public SCimilarity annotation model. To do the same, download and extract it once:

shell
mkdir -p external
curl -L "https://zenodo.org/records/8286452/files/annotation_model_v1.tar.gz?download=1" \
  -o external/annotation_model_v1.tar.gz
tar -xzf external/annotation_model_v1.tar.gz -C external

Without that folder the VAE starts from random weights, which works but is not the setting of the paper.

python
scimilarity = SCIMILARITY_DIR if SCIMILARITY_DIR.is_dir() else None
print("RNA VAE starts from:", "SCimilarity" if scimilarity else "random weights")

autoencoder = WORK / "autoencoder" / "autoencoder.pt"
if not autoencoder.exists():
    mf.train_autoencoder(train, autoencoder.parent, device=DEVICE, **AUTOENCODER)

rna_vae = WORK / "rna_vae" / "rna_vae.pt"
if not rna_vae.exists():
    mf.train_rna_vae(
        train,
        rna_vae.parent,
        scimilarity_model_dir=scimilarity,
        device=DEVICE,
        **RNA_VAE,
    )

encoded = WORK / "train_encoded.h5mu"
if not encoded.exists():
    mf.encode(
        train,
        encoded,
        task="generation",
        autoencoder=autoencoder,
        rna_vae=rna_vae,
        device=DEVICE,
    )

3. Train MultiFlow#

One flow per modality, coupled by cross-attention and conditioned on the cell type.

python
run = WORK / "multiflow"
if not (run / "model.pt").exists():
    mf.train(encoded, run, model="cell-state", device=DEVICE, **FLOW)

4. Generate paired cells#

For every cell type we generate as many cells as were held out (at most 200), with 100 integration steps, and decode them with the decoders that belong to the two encoders. RNA comes out as log-normalised expression, ATAC as binary accessibility.

python
held_out = mf.read_obs(test)["cell_type"].astype(str).value_counts()
n_cells = held_out.clip(upper=200).to_dict()

latent = WORK / "generated_latent.h5mu"
if not latent.exists():
    mf.generate(run, latent, n=n_cells, device=DEVICE)

profiles = WORK / "generated_profiles.h5mu"
if not profiles.exists():
    mf.decode(
        latent,
        profiles,
        task="generation",
        reference=encoded,
        autoencoder=autoencoder,
        rna_vae=rna_vae,
        device=DEVICE,
    )
print(f"{sum(n_cells.values()):,} generated cells of {len(n_cells)} cell types")
4,014 generated cells of 22 cell types

5. Metrics#

Generated and held-out cells are matched by cell type and compared per modality:

  • pcc, scc: Pearson and Spearman correlation of the mean profiles;
  • mmd, mmd_multiscale: maximum mean discrepancy on 50 principal components, with one Gaussian kernel or with the five kernels of the scDiffusion-X evaluation (lower is better);
  • knn_mixing: how evenly real and generated cells mix among the 90 nearest neighbours (0 to 1, higher is better);
  • ilisi: the scIB iLISI, added when the optional package scib is installed.
python
use_ilisi = mf.metrics.scib_available()
table = mf.metrics.evaluate_generation(test, profiles, ilisi=use_ilisi)
table.to_csv(WORK / "generation_metrics.csv")
table.round(4)
n_cell_types n_real n_generated pcc scc mmd mmd_multiscale knn_mixing ilisi
modality
rna 22 3691 3691 0.9979 0.9897 0.0041 0.0410 0.6060 0.9010
atac 22 3691 3691 0.9952 0.9765 0.0037 0.0185 0.9351 0.9074

For comparison, Fig. 2 of the paper reports for MultiFlow:

PCC SCC MMD iLISI
RNA 0.998 0.992 0.015 0.90
ATAC 0.994 0.973 0.006 0.92

A new training run does not reproduce these digits exactly: the encoders are retrained, the held-out cells differ, and MMD depends on the estimator and on the cells that are sampled.

6. A look at the cells (optional)#

Mean profiles of generated against held-out cells, and a joint UMAP of the RNA profiles. Needs matplotlib; the UMAP also needs scanpy (pip install "multiflow-omics[notebooks] @ git+https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git").

python
import importlib.util

import mudata as mu
import numpy as np

if importlib.util.find_spec("matplotlib"):
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    real, generated = mu.read_h5mu(test), mu.read_h5mu(profiles)
    real_rna = mf.metrics.log1p_cp10k(real["rna"].X)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
    panels = [
        ("RNA, mean log expression", real_rna, generated["rna"].X),
        ("ATAC, fraction of cells open", real["atac"].X, generated["atac"].X),
    ]
    for ax, (title, observed, sampled) in zip(axes, panels, strict=True):
        x = np.asarray(observed.mean(axis=0)).ravel()
        y = np.asarray(sampled.mean(axis=0)).ravel()
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=3, color="#2a6f97", alpha=0.4, linewidths=0, rasterized=True)
        limit = max(x.max(), y.max())
        ax.plot([0, limit], [0, limit], color="0.4", linewidth=0.8)
        ax.set(title=title, xlabel="held-out cells", ylabel="generated cells")
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(WORK / "mean_profiles.png", dpi=200)
    plt.show()

python
if importlib.util.find_spec("matplotlib") and importlib.util.find_spec("scanpy"):
    import anndata as ad
    import scanpy as sc

    rna = ad.AnnData(np.vstack([real_rna, np.asarray(generated["rna"].X)]))
    rna.obs["source"] = ["held-out"] * real.n_obs + ["generated"] * generated.n_obs
    rna.obs["cell type"] = list(real["rna"].obs["cell_type"].astype(str)) + list(
        generated["rna"].obs["cell_type"].astype(str)
    )
    sc.pp.pca(rna, n_comps=min(50, rna.n_vars - 1))
    sc.pp.neighbors(rna)
    sc.tl.umap(rna)
    sc.pl.umap(rna, color=["source", "cell type"], wspace=0.35, frameon=False)

python
print(f"finished in {(time.time() - started) / 3600:.2f} h")
finished in 1.75 h

Run it as a batch job#

The encoders and the flow train for several hours, so run the notebook as a job. On a Slurm cluster, one command sets up an environment, fetches the data and submits both tutorials:

shell
git clone https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git && cd MultiFlow
SBATCH_ARGS="--partition=gpu --gpus=1" bash tutorials/run_on_slurm.sh
bash tutorials/run_on_slurm.sh status      # progress, and the metric tables once they exist

Set NOTEBOOKS=generation_openproblems to run only this tutorial, OPENPROBLEM_H5MU=/path/to/openproblem_filtered.h5mu to use a copy of the dataset you already have, and PYTHON or CONDA_ENV to name a Python that has PyTorch for the cluster's GPUs. The executed notebook, the metric table and the figures arrive in tutorial_work/results/. Each step writes a file and is skipped when the file exists, so after a time-out the same command continues where the job stopped. All options are in tutorials/README.md.

Without Slurm, copy the notebook to a disk with about 30 GB of space and execute it there; it keeps data/ and runs/ next to itself:

shell
pip install "multiflow-omics[notebooks] @ git+https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git" nbconvert
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace \
  --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=-1 generation_openproblems.ipynb

Settings used in the paper#

Setting Value
RNA encoder 128-d RNA VAE on log1p counts per 10,000; 200,000 steps; hidden layers initialised from SCimilarity
ATAC encoder 128-d ATAC branch of the paired autoencoder, binary input; 300 epochs
Flow width / residual blocks / cross-attention width 512 / 2 per stream / 64
Flow training 1,600 epochs, Adam, learning rate 10−4, batch size 512
Sampling midpoint ODE, 100 steps, batch size 512

These are the values the notebook passes or the defaults of the functions. See Training and sampling for what each setting does, and Outputs for the files to keep with every result.

Tutorial 2 · notebook

Perturbation prediction

Predict the paired RNA and ATAC response to transcription-factor knockouts in cell types the flow has never seen perturbed. The notebook repeats the leave-one-cell-type-out benchmark of Fig. 3a on the GSE274113 Perturb-multiome data and reports the top-100 PCC-delta, delta MSE and MMD. Everything is trained from scratch with the Python API.

Run it yourself This page is the notebook perturbation_gse274113.ipynb, also in the tutorials/ folder of the repository. It needs MultiFlow (installation), a GPU and the 31 GB dataset, which the notebook downloads. Set QUICK = True in its first cell to run the same steps on a small simulated dataset in about a minute on a CPU. On a Slurm cluster, one command runs it as a job.

The run shown here The outputs below come from a run that held out five of the ten cell types in turn: BFU-E, CFU-E, basophilic erythroblasts, EoBasoMast precursors and MEP. The first cell of the notebook names them in CELL_TYPES; with CELL_TYPES = None, as in the notebook you download, every cell type is held out. The means in the results table are therefore means over these five cell types.

Step Function
Download the data mf.download_dataset
Train the paired autoencoder and encode mf.train_autoencoder, mf.encode
Hold out one cell type mf.prepare_perturbation_fold
Train MultiFlow mf.train
Predict every knockout mf.predict_perturbations
Score against the observed cells mf.metrics.evaluate_perturbation
python
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

import multiflow as mf

QUICK = os.environ.get("MULTIFLOW_QUICK") == "1"  # or simply: QUICK = True
DEVICE = None  # None uses the GPU when there is one
CELL_TYPES = ['BFU-E', 'Basophilic Erythroblast', 'CFU-E', 'EoBasoMast Precursor', 'MEP']  # the held-out cell types of this run; None holds out every cell type

if QUICK:  # simulated data and small networks: about a minute on a CPU
    WORK = Path("runs/perturbation_quick")
    AUTOENCODER = dict(epochs=40, rna_dims=(128, 64, 16), atac_dims=(128, 64, 16))
    FLOW = dict(epochs=15, hidden_dim=64, batch_size=64)
else:  # the settings of the paper
    WORK = Path("runs/perturbation")
    AUTOENCODER = dict(epochs=100)
    FLOW = dict(epochs=600)

started = time.time()
print("multiflow-omics", mf.__version__)
multiflow-omics 0.2.0

1. Data#

The processed file is 31 GB (Zenodo). RNA holds raw counts and ATAC is binary; cell_type and perturbation annotate every cell, and unperturbed cells are labelled control. The table lists the number of cells per cell type and perturbation.

python
if QUICK:
    data = WORK / "simulated.h5mu"
    if not data.exists():
        mf.simulate_h5mu(data)
else:
    data = mf.download_dataset(
        "gse274113", "data/GSE274113_filtered.h5mu", accept_license=True
    )

obs = mf.read_obs(data)
cells = (
    obs.astype({"cell_type": str, "perturbation": str})
    .groupby(["cell_type", "perturbation"])
    .size()
    .unstack(fill_value=0)
)
print(f"{len(obs):,} cells, {cells.shape[0]} cell types, {cells.shape[1] - 1} knockouts")
cells
137,604 cells, 11 cell types, 19 knockouts

2. Autoencoder#

For perturbation prediction both modalities go through one paired autoencoder: RNA with a negative-binomial decoder on raw counts, ATAC with a Bernoulli decoder. As in the paper, it is trained once on all cells; the hold-out applies to the flow.

python
autoencoder = WORK / "autoencoder" / "autoencoder.pt"
if not autoencoder.exists():
    mf.train_autoencoder(data, autoencoder.parent, device=DEVICE, **AUTOENCODER)

encoded = WORK / "encoded.h5mu"
if not encoded.exists():
    mf.encode(
        data, encoded, task="perturbation", autoencoder=autoencoder, device=DEVICE
    )

3. Leave one cell type out#

For each held-out cell type:

  1. prepare_perturbation_fold removes its perturbed cells and stores the context of every cell type (the mean latent state of its training cells);
  2. train fits MultiFlow, conditioned on the context and on the perturbation;
  3. predict_perturbations samples as many cells per knockout as were observed, applies the training-only mean shift of the paper (the mean effect of the knockout in the training cell types is added to the control mean of the held-out cell type) and decodes RNA and ATAC;
  4. evaluate_perturbation compares predicted and observed cells.

The metrics use the 100 genes that respond most strongly in the observed data (largest absolute t statistic, knockout against control):

  • pcc_delta: correlation between the predicted and the observed change of the mean expression (higher is better);
  • delta_mse: mean squared difference between the two changes (lower is better);
  • mmd: distance between predicted and observed cells (lower is better);
  • ilisi: the scIB iLISI, added when the optional package scib is installed.

Every step writes a file and is skipped when that file exists, so an interrupted run continues where it stopped.

python
held_out = CELL_TYPES or [name for name in cells.index if name.lower() != "nan"]
use_ilisi = mf.metrics.scib_available()
tables = []

for cell_type in held_out:
    folder = WORK / "folds" / cell_type.replace("/", "-").replace(" ", "_")
    fold, run = folder / "fold.h5mu", folder / "multiflow"
    predicted, result = folder / "predicted.h5mu", folder / "metrics.csv"

    if not predicted.exists():
        fold_started = time.time()
        if not fold.exists():
            mf.prepare_perturbation_fold(encoded, fold, held_out_cell_type=cell_type)
        if not (run / "model.pt").exists():
            mf.train(
                fold,
                run,
                model="perturbation",
                perturbation_key="perturbation",
                device=DEVICE,
                verbose=False,
                **FLOW,
            )
        observed = cells.loc[cell_type].drop("control")
        mf.predict_perturbations(
            run,
            predicted,
            training_fold=fold,
            held_out_cell_type=cell_type,
            autoencoder=autoencoder,
            n_cells=observed[observed >= 5].to_dict(),
            device=DEVICE,
        )
        fold.unlink()  # as large as the data, and not needed again
        minutes = (time.time() - fold_started) / 60
        print(f"{cell_type}: trained and predicted in {minutes:.1f} min")

    if not result.exists():
        mf.metrics.evaluate_perturbation(
            data, predicted, cell_type=cell_type, ilisi=use_ilisi
        ).to_csv(result, index=False)
    tables.append(pd.read_csv(result))

metrics = pd.concat(tables, ignore_index=True)
metrics.to_csv(WORK / "perturbation_metrics.csv", index=False)
print(f"{len(metrics)} cell type and perturbation pairs")
95 cell type and perturbation pairs

4. Results#

Mean over the perturbations of each held-out cell type, and the mean over all pairs.

python
columns = [c for c in ("pcc_delta", "delta_mse", "mmd", "ilisi") if c in metrics]
summary = metrics.groupby("cell_type")[columns].mean()
summary.loc["all pairs"] = metrics[columns].mean()
summary.round(3)

5. A look at the pairs (optional)#

One point per perturbation; the bar marks the mean of the cell type. Needs matplotlib.

python
import importlib.util

import numpy as np

if importlib.util.find_spec("matplotlib"):
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    order = summary.drop("all pairs")["pcc_delta"].sort_values(ascending=False).index
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(max(4.0, 0.7 * len(order) + 1.5), 3.4))
    for position, name in enumerate(order):
        values = metrics.loc[metrics["cell_type"] == name, "pcc_delta"].to_numpy()
        jitter = rng.uniform(-0.18, 0.18, size=values.size)
        x = position + jitter
        ax.scatter(x, values, s=14, color="#2a6f97", alpha=0.7, linewidths=0)
        ax.hlines(values.mean(), position - 0.3, position + 0.3, color="#182f40", lw=2)
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.6", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(order)), order, rotation=45, ha="right")
    ax.set_ylabel("top-100 PCC-delta")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(WORK / "pcc_delta_by_cell_type.png", dpi=200)
    plt.show()

python
print(f"finished in {(time.time() - started) / 3600:.2f} h")
finished in 0.01 h

The training-only mean shift#

Before decoding, predict_perturbations moves each generated group to a target mean that is computed from training cells only. For each modality, with latent states z:

Δ = mean(z | perturbation p, training cells) − mean(z | control, training cells)
target = mean(z | control, held-out cell type) + α Δ
zgenerated ← zgenerated − mean(zgenerated) + target

The default alpha=1 uses the full training effect, and debias=False switches the shift off. No perturbed cell of the held-out cell type is used. The same step is available on its own as mf.debias_perturbation.

One knockout at a time#

predict_perturbations is the three steps below, repeated for every knockout with the fold read once:

python
latent = mf.generate(run, "latent.h5mu", n=500, cell_type="Basophilic Erythroblast",
                     perturbation="GATA1")
shifted = mf.debias_perturbation(latent, "latent_shifted.h5mu", training_fold=fold,
                                 held_out_cell_type="Basophilic Erythroblast",
                                 perturbation="GATA1")
profiles = mf.decode(shifted, "profiles.h5mu", task="perturbation", reference=fold,
                     autoencoder=autoencoder)

Use the cell-type and perturbation names exactly as they are stored in the file; the table at the start of the notebook lists them.

Run it as a batch job#

The full run trains one autoencoder and one flow per held-out cell type, so run the notebook as a job. On a Slurm cluster, one command sets up an environment, fetches the data and submits both tutorials:

shell
git clone https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git && cd MultiFlow
SBATCH_ARGS="--partition=gpu --gpus=1" bash tutorials/run_on_slurm.sh
bash tutorials/run_on_slurm.sh status      # progress, and the metric tables once they exist

Set NOTEBOOKS=perturbation_gse274113 to run only this tutorial, GSE274113_H5MU=/path/to/GSE274113_filtered.h5mu to use a copy of the dataset you already have, and PYTHON or CONDA_ENV to name a Python that has PyTorch for the cluster's GPUs. The job asks for 200 GB of memory by default, because the 31 GB dataset is read into memory. The executed notebook, the metric table and the figure arrive in tutorial_work/results/. Each step writes a file and is skipped when the file exists, so after a time-out the same command continues where the job stopped. To shorten the run, set CELL_TYPES in the first cell to a few cell types. All options are in tutorials/README.md.

Without Slurm, copy the notebook to a disk with about 100 GB of space and execute it there; it keeps data/ and runs/ next to itself:

shell
pip install "multiflow-omics[notebooks] @ git+https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git" nbconvert
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace \
  --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=-1 perturbation_gse274113.ipynb

Encoder and held-out cells As in the paper, one autoencoder is fitted on all cells and the hold-out applies to flow training only. If the encoder should not see the held-out cell type either, remove its perturbed cells from the raw file first and train one autoencoder per fold.

Settings used in the paper#

Setting Generation Perturbation

RNA encoder input log1p counts per 10,000 raw counts
ATAC encoder 128-d ATAC branch, binary input same
Autoencoder epochs 300 100
Flow width / blocks / cross-attention width 512 / 2 / 64 512 / 2 / 64
Flow epochs 1,600 600
Batch size, Adam learning rate 512, 10−4 512, 10−4
Midpoint ODE steps 100 50
Sampling batch size 512 256

User guide

Data format

MultiFlow reads and writes paired cells as H5MU files: one MuData container with an rna and an atac modality. The package checks the pairing and the matrix scales and never guesses preprocessing.

The input you provide#

paired.h5mu
├── rna.X                        non-negative integer RNA counts
├── atac.X                       binary ATAC accessibility (0 or 1)
├── rna.obs["cell_type"]         cell-type name, no missing values
├── rna.obs["perturbation"]      perturbation input only; includes "control"
└── rna.obs_names == atac.obs_names   unique, same values in the same order

Audit any file before training:

python
report = mf.validate_h5mu("paired.h5mu")
report["paired_raw_contract_ok"]      # True: raw RNA counts, binary ATAC, paired cells
shell
multiflow data validate paired.h5mu --json report.json   # the same report, as a file

mf.read_obs("paired.h5mu") returns the cell annotations without loading the matrices, and mf.simulate_h5mu writes a small file in this format to experiment with.

The report lists, for each matrix, its shape, range, whether it is finite, integer-like, non-negative and binary, and whether it meets the contract. latent_ready says whether the latent representations described below are present.

Latent representations#

The flow is trained on 128-dimensional encoder states, not on raw matrices. mf.encode creates them with the encoders you trained (mf.train_autoencoder, and mf.train_rna_vae for generation) and stores them in rna.obsm["X_multiflow"] and atac.obsm["X_multiflow"]. They are intermediate data; you are not expected to supply them by hand.

Task Modality Encoder Encoder input Decoder output
Generation RNA RNA VAE normalised 104 + log1p normalised log-expression
Generation ATAC paired autoencoder, ATAC branch binary Bernoulli sample (0/1)
Perturbation RNA paired autoencoder, RNA branch raw counts sampled counts
Perturbation ATAC paired autoencoder, ATAC branch binary Bernoulli sample (0/1)

Use rna_representation and atac_representation of mf.train to train on another obsm key. X can be chosen explicitly, but it is never used as a silent fallback when a latent key is missing.

Scales are stated, not guessed#

The RNA VAE and the paired autoencoder use different input and output scales. mf.encode records the items below in the encoded file; if you bring your own encoder, state them yourself:

  1. the input matrix or layer and its scale;
  2. the feature identifiers, in exact order;
  3. checkpoint and configuration hashes;
  4. the latent dimension and the encoder's scale factors;
  5. the decoder's output scale; and
  6. whether the encoder was trained on the training split only.

On top of the encoder, MultiFlow fits a feature-wise latent standardiser on the training cells. The standardiser and the mapping from names to integer labels are stored in model.pt and run.json.

Perturbation inputs#

  • The perturbation column (default perturbation) must contain the control condition (default control). It is reserved as index 0 and contributes an exactly zero perturbation embedding.
  • The context matrix is stored in uns["multiflow_context_matrix"], with its row names in uns["multiflow_context_classes"]. The names must match the cell-type classes in the same order; MultiFlow rejects missing or reordered rows. mf.prepare_perturbation_fold writes both.

Generated files#

mf.generate writes paired latent states to rna.X and atac.X, marked uns["matrix_scale"] = "latent", and records in mdata.uns["multiflow"]:

Key Content
checkpoint_sha256 hash of the model file that produced the cells
model_config model type and sizes
seed, ode_steps, batch_size, rng_mode everything that determines the random draws
label_classes, perturbation_classes the name ↔ index mappings
standardization_inverted whether the latent standardiser was undone

mf.decode then turns the latent states into profiles with the encoders that were used to encode the training data: RNA as a dense matrix, binary ATAC as a sparse one, with uns["matrix_scale"] naming the scale. mf.predict_perturbations writes the same kind of file for several perturbations at once, with a perturbation column in obs. A decoder must never be taken from an unrelated file.

PreviousPerturbation predictionNextModels

User guide

Models

MultiFlow is a flow-matching model on paired latent states. One network predicts two velocities, one for RNA and one for ATAC, and the two streams exchange information through bidirectional cross-attention, so the modalities are integrated as one coupled system.

Three architectures#

Name Class Command option Use
MultiFlow CellStateFlow --model cell-state (default) Generate cells of a named cell type.
MultiFlowPerturbation PerturbationFlow --model perturbation Predict the response to a perturbation in a cell context.
MultiFlowConcat ConditionalConcatFlow --model concat Concatenation ablation, kept to reproduce the benchmark.

The vector field#

  • Each stream is projected to a hidden width of 512 and passes through two residual blocks, a middle block and two more residual blocks, with skip connections between them. The same residual blocks process both streams.
  • Every residual block is modulated by the condition, the sum of a sinusoidal time embedding and the label embedding, through a scale and a shift.
  • Three cross-flow modules (CFM1–CFM3) couple the streams. In each one, RNA queries attend to ATAC keys and values, and ATAC queries attend to RNA keys and values.

Feature-level cross-attention#

Each modality enters a cross-flow module as a single token whose channels are its 512 hidden features. Attention is computed between features, not between cells or sequence positions:

AR←A = softmax( qR kA⊤ / √64 ),   hR ← hR + WR AR←A vA
AA←R = softmax( qA kR⊤ / √64 ),   hA ← hA + WA AA←R vR

Here every hidden feature gets a 64-dimensional query, key and value. Each attention matrix is therefore 512 × 512, one row per feature of one modality and one column per feature of the other. The Attention Explorer shows these maps for CFM2.

Conditioning#

  • Cell state. num_classes cell types, each with a learned embedding added to the time embedding.
  • Perturbation. A context embedding and a perturbation embedding replace the class embedding. The context embedding is taken from a fixed matrix, by default the mean encoder state of each cell type (frozen during training, freeze_context=True); its width must equal the hidden width or half of it. Perturbation index 0 is the control; its embedding is exactly zero and receives no gradient. Time, context and perturbation embeddings are each layer-normalised before they are added.

The flow objective#

For a target paired state x1 = (x1R, x1A), MultiFlow draws one Gaussian source over the concatenated RNA–ATAC space and a time t uniformly from (0, 1), and regresses the velocity of the straight path between them:

x0 = (x0R, x0A) ~ N(0, IdR+dA),   xt = (1 − t) x0 + t x1,   vt = x1 − x0
loss = ‖ v̂R(xt, t, c) − vtR ‖² + ‖ v̂A(xt, t, c) − vtA ‖²

The RNA and ATAC blocks of the source are independent coordinates of one full-rank random variable. Their dependence at the end point is learned by the coupled vector field, not imposed by the source. The concatenation ablation keeps its historical shared source only to reproduce the benchmark.

Choosing sizes#

Parameter Default Paper Effect
hidden_dim 512 512 width of each stream; also the size of the attention maps
num_blocks 2 2 residual blocks before and after the middle block
cross_attention_dim 64 64 query/key/value width per feature
num_layers (concat only) 8 — depth of the concatenation network

Feature-level attention costs grow with the square of hidden_dim; sampling the default model on a CPU is slow, so use a GPU for real data or a smaller width for tests.

PreviousData formatNextTraining and sampling

User guide

Training and sampling

How MultiFlow fits the vector field, how it integrates it to produce cells, and which settings decide whether a result can be reproduced exactly.

Training#

Each epoch shuffles the paired cells and, for every mini-batch, draws a joint Gaussian source and a flow time per cell, builds the straight-line state and regresses its velocity (objective). The optimiser is Adam. The loss history is returned by fit and written to history.csv by the command line.

TrainingConfig field Default Meaning
epochs 600 passes over the training cells
batch_size 512 cells per optimisation step
learning_rate 1e-4 Adam step size
seed 0 seed of the training stream
device cuda if available, else cpu where training runs
standardize True standardise each latent feature on the training cells
noise_mode auto source distribution; auto picks the one the model requires
reseed True fit reseeds before training; the CLI seeds once before building the model and sets this to False

Latent standardisation#

With standardize=True, fit estimates a mean and a standard deviation for every RNA and ATAC latent feature on the training cells and trains on the standardised values. The fitted LatentStandardizer is returned in TrainingResult.standardizer, saved in the checkpoint, and inverted after sampling. It sits on top of the encoder's own scaling and does not replace it.

Seeds#

For an exact rerun through the Python API, call seed_everything(seed) before building the model, so that the initial weights are reproducible as well. The command line does this for you.

Sampling#

sample_paired_latents integrates the learned vector field from the Gaussian source at t = 0 to t = 1 with the explicit midpoint rule. At each step the RNA and ATAC velocities are evaluated together, so each modality's update depends on the other's current state.

Setting Generation Perturbation
ODE steps (steps, --steps) 100 50
batch size 512 256

The command line takes the step count saved with the run (--sampling-steps at training time) unless --steps is given, and records the value in the output.

Random-number modes#

rng_mode What it does When to use it
joint (default) draws one full-rank Gaussian over the concatenated RNA–ATAC space per batch and splits it into the two blocks all new work
batch_invariant draws the whole initial state first, so a seed gives the same cells for any batch size comparing runs with different batch sizes; uses memory proportional to the number of cells
legacy_interleaved reproduces the historical two-call RNA/ATAC draw order reproducing archived results only

Record the seed, batch size, number of steps, device and package version with every result: together they determine the sampled cells. Generated H5MU files store all of them.

Perturbation prediction#

For the perturbation model, give the cell context and the perturbation by name (--cell-type, --perturbation) or by index (label, perturbation). The control, index 0, has a zero perturbation embedding, so sampling with the control gives the model's control cells for that context. The paper then applies the training-only mean shift before decoding.

PreviousModelsNextOutputs and reproducibility

User guide

Outputs and reproducibility

Every run writes its model together with the settings and hashes needed to reproduce it. This page lists what is written where, and what to keep.

The run directory#

mf.train(..., "runs/name") creates a new directory:

File Content
model.pt portable checkpoint: model configuration and weights, latent standardiser, optimiser state, epoch, loss history and metadata
run.json manifest: package version, input file and its size (and SHA256 with --hash-input), H5MU contract (keys and number of paired cells), label and perturbation classes, model configuration, training settings, default sampling steps, checkpoint SHA256
history.csv one row per epoch: epoch, loss_rna, loss_atac, loss_total
shell
multiflow inspect --checkpoint runs/name/model.pt

prints the stored metadata without loading the data.

Encoders and intermediate files#

Written by Files Content
mf.split_h5mu train.h5mu, test.h5mu, split_manifest.csv, split_metadata.json the two parts, the cell-by-cell assignment, the seed and the checksum of the source
mf.train_autoencoder autoencoder.pt, autoencoder_training.json weights and layer widths; settings, loss history and the checksum of the training file
mf.train_rna_vae rna_vae.pt, rna_vae_training.json weights; settings and the checksum of the training file
mf.encode encoded H5MU the input plus X_multiflow in both modalities; uns["multiflow_encoder"] holds the task, the encoder checksums and the scale factors
mf.prepare_perturbation_fold fold H5MU the training cells of one fold, the context matrix and uns["multiflow_fold"]
mf.decode, mf.predict_perturbations profile H5MU RNA and ATAC profiles; uns records the checkpoints, the seed and, for predictions, the mean-shift settings

Checkpoints#

  • save_checkpoint writes atomically, so an interrupted save never leaves a half-written file.
  • load_checkpoint rebuilds the model from its stored configuration and returns (model, standardizer, metadata). It loads with PyTorch's safe weights-only loader.
  • Checkpoints from the original research scripts use other layouts. Convert a trusted one once with multiflow migrate or migrate_legacy_checkpoint; pass --trust-source only for a file whose origin you have checked, because it allows PyTorch's unrestricted loader.
shell
multiflow migrate --source old_model.pt --output model.pt \
  --model-type perturbation \
  --standardizer-npz latent_stats.npz \
  --label-classes "BFU-E" "CFU-E" "Pro-E" \
  --perturbation-classes control GATA1 TAL1

Reproducibility checklist#

Keep these with every result; run.json and the H5MU metadata already record most of them.

  1. Checksum of the raw H5MU and the split manifest.
  2. Exact feature order and matrix scales.
  3. Encoder checkpoints with their hashes and scale factors.
  4. Flow latent statistics (the standardiser) and the label mappings.
  5. Training settings and sampling settings: seed, batch size, ODE steps, device, random-number mode, package version.

Never swap a decoder A decoder is only valid for the encoder that produced the training latents. Do not exchange a decoder checkpoint after the flow has been trained.

PreviousTraining and samplingNextFAQ and troubleshooting

User guide

FAQ and troubleshooting

Answers to the questions and error messages that come up most often, and a short glossary of the terms used in these pages.

Running#

Sampling on a CPU is very slow#

Each cross-flow module computes a 512 × 512 attention matrix for every cell at every integration step, so a full-size model needs a GPU for real data. To check an installation on a CPU, train a small model with hidden_dim=64, as in the quick start, and generate a few hundred cells.

I run out of GPU memory#

Lower batch_size for training or generation. The cells are integrated batch by batch, so a smaller batch only takes longer. With --rng-mode batch_invariant the whole initial state is drawn at once, which uses memory in proportion to the number of cells; use the default joint mode for large runs.

"unknown cell-type … choose from […]"#

Cell types and perturbations are given by name, exactly as they were spelled in the training file. The error lists the valid names; they are also stored in run.json (label_classes, perturbation_classes) and printed by multiflow inspect --checkpoint runs/name/model.pt.

Do I need scDiffusion-X, Scanpy or scvi-tools?#

No. Since version 0.2 the paired autoencoder is part of the package, in plain PyTorch, and the built-in metrics need only NumPy and SciPy. Checkpoints that were trained with scDiffusion-X still load: pass the .ckpt file as autoencoder. Scanpy and scib are optional, for the figures in the notebooks and for the scIB iLISI.

How long do the tutorials take?#

In quick mode, about a minute each on a CPU. With the paper settings they train for hours on a GPU: the generation tutorial trains two encoders and one flow for 1,600 epochs, and the perturbation tutorial trains one autoencoder and one flow per held-out cell type. Both can be interrupted and resumed.

Data#

validate reports contract_ok: false#

The input must hold raw, paired profiles:

  • rna.X with non-negative integer counts, not normalised values;
  • atac.X with only 0 and 1; binarise a count matrix first;
  • the same cells in the same order in both modalities (obs_names identical).

The report names the matrix and the property that failed (finite, integer-like, non-negative or binary).

latent_ready: false#

The file has no latent representations yet. Run mf.encode (see the quick start), or point mf.train to existing keys with rna_representation and atac_representation. MultiFlow never falls back to X silently.

Can I use my own encoder?#

Yes. Store the paired latent states in rna.obsm and atac.obsm under any key and pass the keys to train. MultiFlow does not guess preprocessing, so keep the encoder's scale factors and decode the generated latents with the decoder that belongs to the same encoder.

A dataset download stopped halfway#

Call mf.download_dataset (or multiflow data download) again: it resumes the transfer and checks the size and MD5 before it writes the final file. force=True starts again from scratch.

Results#

How do I reproduce a result exactly?#

Keep the seed, batch size, number of ODE steps, device, random-number mode and package version. Generated files store all of them in uns["multiflow"]. Use --rng-mode batch_invariant if you need the same cells for different batch sizes. See Outputs and reproducibility.

Why does the perturbation workflow shift the generated mean?#

For a cell type the flow has never seen perturbed, the paper corrects the mean of the generated group with the perturbation effect estimated on the training cells. No perturbed cell of the held-out type is used. The formula is on the perturbation tutorial.

I have checkpoints from the original research scripts#

Convert each trusted file once with multiflow migrate (or migrate_legacy_checkpoint in Python), giving the label and perturbation names in order. See Checkpoints.

Glossary#

Term Meaning
H5MU MuData file holding the paired rna and atac modalities of the same cells
X_multiflow the 128-dimensional encoder state of each modality, stored in obsm
Context a cell type the perturbation model is conditioned on, given by a row of the context matrix
Control perturbation index 0; its embedding is exactly zero
Cross-flow module (CFM) one bidirectional cross-attention layer between the RNA and ATAC streams; MultiFlow has three
Leave-one-cell-type-out (LOCO) training without the perturbed cells of one cell type, then predicting them
Standardiser per-feature mean and standard deviation of the training latents, inverted after sampling
Midpoint ODE steps number of integration steps from noise to cells: 100 for generation, 50 for perturbation
PreviousOutputs and reproducibilityNextPython API

Reference

Python API

The public objects of multiflow 0.2.0. Everything is imported from the package root; the metrics live in multiflow.metrics. The Workflow functions are the ones the tutorials use: each reads and writes files and returns the path it wrote.

python
import multiflow as mf

Workflow#

functiondownload_datasetmultiflow

download_dataset(name, output, *, accept_license, force=False) -> Path

Download one of the two datasets of the paper, resuming an interrupted transfer, and check its size and MD5 before the file appears at output. An existing file is verified and returned.

Parameters
name
"openproblem" (8.4 GB, CC BY 4.0) or "gse274113" (31 GB).
output
where to store the H5MU file.
accept_license
must be True; confirms that you have read the terms of the source.
force · default False
download again even if the file exists.
Example
python
data = mf.download_dataset("openproblem", "data/openproblem_filtered.h5mu", accept_license=True)

functionsplit_h5mumultiflow

split_h5mu(input, output_dir, *, condition_key="cell_type", train_fraction=0.8, seed=20260717) -> tuple[Path, Path]

Split raw paired profiles into train.h5mu and test.h5mu, stratified by cell type. Also writes split_manifest.csv and split_metadata.json. Split before any encoder is trained.

Parameters
input
raw paired H5MU file.
output_dir
new or empty folder for the two files.
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type.
train_fraction · default 0.8
share of the cells of every cell type that goes to the training file.
seed · default 20260717
random seed.
Returns

The paths of the training and the test file.

functiontrain_autoencodermultiflow

train_autoencoder(input, output_dir, *, condition_key="cell_type", epochs=300, batch_size=256, rna_dims=(512, 300, 128), atac_dims=(1024, 512, 128), seed=20260717, device=None, verbose=True) -> Path

Train the paired RNA/ATAC autoencoder on raw profiles. RNA is reconstructed with a negative-binomial likelihood on raw counts, ATAC with a Bernoulli likelihood on binary accessibility. Writes autoencoder.pt and autoencoder_training.json into output_dir.

Parameters
input
raw paired H5MU file (training cells).
output_dir
folder for the checkpoint.
epochs · default 300
training epochs; the paper uses 300 for generation and 100 for perturbation prediction.
batch_size · default 256
cells per batch.
rna_dims · default (512, 300, 128)
widths of the RNA encoder; the last number is the latent width. The decoder mirrors it.
atac_dims · default (1024, 512, 128)
the same for ATAC.
seed · default 20260717
random seed.
device · default None
"cuda" or "cpu"; None uses the GPU when there is one.
verbose · default True
print the progress.
Returns

The path of autoencoder.pt.

Example
python
autoencoder = mf.train_autoencoder("train.h5mu", "runs/autoencoder", epochs=300)

functiontrain_rna_vaemultiflow

train_rna_vae(input, output_dir, *, scimilarity_model_dir=None, max_steps=200000, checkpoint_every=50000, batch_size=128, seed=1234, device=None, verbose=True) -> Path

Train the RNA VAE used for cell-state generation, on log1p counts per 10,000: three 1,024-unit layers and a 128-dimensional, L2-normalised latent state. Writes rna_vae.pt and rna_vae_training.json.

Parameters
input
raw paired H5MU file (training cells).
output_dir
folder for the checkpoint.
scimilarity_model_dir · default None
folder of the SCimilarity annotation model; its weights initialise the hidden layers, as in the paper. None starts from random weights.
max_steps · default 200000
optimisation steps.
checkpoint_every · default 50000
also save an intermediate checkpoint every so many steps; 0 switches this off.
batch_size · default 128
cells per batch.
seed · default 1234
random seed.
device · default None
"cuda" or "cpu"; None uses the GPU when there is one.
verbose · default True
print the progress.
Returns

The path of rna_vae.pt.

functionencodemultiflow

encode(input, output, *, task, autoencoder, rna_vae=None, condition_key="cell_type", batch_size=2048, device=None) -> Path

Encode raw profiles into the latent states MultiFlow is trained on, and store them in rna.obsm["X_multiflow"] and atac.obsm["X_multiflow"] of a copy of the input, together with the checksums and scale factors of the encoders.

Parameters
input
raw paired H5MU file.
output
encoded H5MU file to write.
task
"generation": RNA through the RNA VAE, ATAC through the autoencoder; "perturbation": both modalities through the autoencoder.
autoencoder
checkpoint written by train_autoencoder.
rna_vae · default None
checkpoint written by train_rna_vae; needed for generation.
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type.
batch_size · default 2048
cells encoded at a time.
device · default None
"cuda" or "cpu"; None uses the GPU when there is one.
Example
python
encoded = mf.encode("train.h5mu", "train_encoded.h5mu", task="generation",
                    autoencoder=autoencoder, rna_vae=rna_vae)

functiontrainmultiflow

train(input, output, *, model="cell-state", condition_key="cell_type", perturbation_key=None, control_perturbation="control", epochs=600, batch_size=512, learning_rate=0.0001, hidden_dim=512, num_blocks=2, num_layers=8, cross_attention_dim=64, sampling_steps=None, standardize=True, seed=0, device=None, hash_input=False, verbose=True) -> Path

Train MultiFlow on an encoded H5MU file and write a run folder with model.pt, history.csv and run.json. The latent states are standardised on the training cells; the statistics are saved with the model and undone after sampling.

Parameters
input
encoded H5MU file, or a fold written by prepare_perturbation_fold.
output
new run folder.
model · default "cell-state"
"cell-state" (generation), "perturbation" or "concat" (the ablation without cross-attention).
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type. None trains without labels.
perturbation_key · default None
column of rna.obs with the perturbation. Required for the perturbation model.
control_perturbation · default "control"
name of the unperturbed condition.
epochs · default 600
training epochs; the paper uses 1600 for generation and 600 for perturbation prediction.
batch_size · default 512
cells per batch.
learning_rate · default 0.0001
Adam learning rate.
hidden_dim · default 512
width of each stream. For the perturbation model it must equal the width of the context (RNA plus ATAC latent width) or twice that.
num_blocks · default 2
residual blocks per stream.
num_layers · default 8
depth of the concat model.
cross_attention_dim · default 64
query, key and value width per hidden feature.
sampling_steps · default None
default number of integration steps stored with the run; None stores 100 for generation and 50 for perturbation prediction.
standardize · default True
standardise each latent feature on the training cells.
seed · default 0
random seed.
device · default None
"cuda" or "cpu"; None uses the GPU when there is one.
hash_input · default False
record the SHA-256 of the input file in run.json.
verbose · default True
print the losses about ten times.
Returns

The path of the run folder.

Example
python
run = mf.train("train_encoded.h5mu", "runs/multiflow", model="cell-state", epochs=1600)

functiongeneratemultiflow

generate(run, output, *, n, cell_type=None, perturbation=None, steps=None, batch_size=512, seed=0, device=None, keep_standardized=False, rng_mode="joint") -> Path

Sample paired latent states from a trained run and write them as an H5MU file with everything needed to reproduce them (checkpoint checksum, seed, integration steps, batch size).

Parameters
run
run folder or checkpoint file.
output
H5MU file to write.
n
number of cells for cell_type, or a mapping from cell type to number of cells; the cell types of a mapping go into one file.
cell_type · default None
cell type to generate, by name.
perturbation · default None
perturbation, by name (perturbation models).
steps · default None
midpoint integration steps; None uses the number stored with the run.
batch_size · default 512
cells integrated at a time.
seed · default 0
random seed.
device · default None
"cuda" or "cpu"; None uses the GPU when there is one.
keep_standardized · default False
return the standardised latent states instead of undoing the standardisation.
rng_mode · default "joint"
"joint", "legacy_interleaved" or "batch_invariant"; see sample_paired_latents.
Example
python
latent = mf.generate(run, "generated_latent.h5mu", n={"CD14+ Mono": 200, "NK": 200})

functiondecodemultiflow

decode(input, output, *, task, reference, autoencoder, rna_vae=None, condition_key="cell_type", batch_size=2048, seed=0, device=None) -> Path

Decode generated latent states into RNA and ATAC profiles with the decoders that belong to the encoders. For generation, RNA is a log1p CP10k reconstruction; for perturbation prediction, RNA is a count drawn from the negative binomial of the autoencoder. ATAC is a binary sample, stored sparse.

Parameters
input
latent H5MU written by generate.
output
profile H5MU to write.
task
"generation" or "perturbation", as in encode.
reference
the encoded training file (or fold); it provides the feature names, the scale factors and, for perturbation prediction, the library sizes.
autoencoder
the autoencoder checkpoint used for encoding.
rna_vae · default None
the RNA VAE checkpoint used for encoding (generation).
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type.
batch_size · default 2048
cells decoded at a time.
seed · default 0
seed of the binary ATAC sample and of the library sizes.
device · default None
"cuda" or "cpu"; None uses the GPU when there is one.

functionprepare_perturbation_foldmultiflow

prepare_perturbation_fold(input, output, *, held_out_cell_type, condition_key="cell_type", perturbation_key="perturbation", control_perturbation="control") -> Path

Build one leave-one-cell-type-out fold from an encoded file: remove every perturbed cell of the held-out cell type, keep its control cells, and store the context of each cell type (the mean latent state of its training cells).

Parameters
input
encoded H5MU file.
output
fold H5MU to write.
held_out_cell_type
name of the cell type to hold out.
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type.
perturbation_key · default "perturbation"
column of rna.obs with the perturbation.
control_perturbation · default "control"
name of the unperturbed condition.

functionpredict_perturbationsmultiflow

predict_perturbations(run, output, *, training_fold, held_out_cell_type, autoencoder, n_cells, perturbations=None, condition_key="cell_type", perturbation_key="perturbation", control_perturbation="control", debias=True, alpha=1.0, min_cells=5, steps=None, batch_size=256, seed=0, device=None) -> Path

Predict the RNA and ATAC profiles of a held-out cell type under several perturbations in one pass: sample latent states, apply the training-only mean shift and decode. The result is one H5MU file whose obs has cell_type and perturbation.

Parameters
run
run folder of a perturbation model.
output
profile H5MU to write.
training_fold
the fold the run was trained on.
held_out_cell_type
cell type to predict.
autoencoder
the autoencoder checkpoint used for encoding.
n_cells
number of cells per perturbation: one number for all, or a mapping from perturbation to number.
perturbations · default None
perturbations to predict; default: the keys of the mapping, or every perturbation of the run except the control.
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type.
perturbation_key · default "perturbation"
column of rna.obs with the perturbation.
control_perturbation · default "control"
name of the unperturbed condition.
debias · default True
apply the mean shift (the protocol of the paper).
alpha · default 1.0
share of the training effect that is added.
min_cells · default 5
smallest group of training cells accepted for the mean shift.
steps · default None
integration steps; None uses the number stored with the run (50).
batch_size · default 256
cells integrated at a time.
seed · default 0
perturbation i is sampled with seed + i.
device · default None
"cuda" or "cpu"; None uses the GPU when there is one.
Example
python
predicted = mf.predict_perturbations(run, "predicted.h5mu", training_fold=fold,
                                     held_out_cell_type="Pro-E", autoencoder=autoencoder,
                                     n_cells={"GATA1": 500, "TAL1": 500})

functiondebias_perturbationmultiflow

debias_perturbation(input, output, *, training_fold, held_out_cell_type, perturbation, condition_key="cell_type", perturbation_key="perturbation", control_perturbation="control", alpha=1.0, min_cells=5) -> Path

Apply the training-only mean shift to one generated latent file. predict_perturbations does this for you; use this function to run the steps one at a time.

held_out_cell_type
the held-out cell type.
perturbation
the perturbation of the generated cells.
alpha · default 1.0
share of the training effect that is added.
min_cells · default 5
smallest group of training cells accepted.

Metrics#

functionmetrics.evaluate_generationmultiflow

evaluate_generation(real, generated, *, condition_key="cell_type", max_per_label=200, max_total=4000, ilisi=False, seed=0) -> DataFrame

The generation metrics of the paper for RNA and ATAC. The same number of observed and generated cells is drawn for every cell type; RNA is compared on log1p CP10k, ATAC as binary accessibility.

Parameters
real
observed raw profiles: path of an H5MU file, or a MuData.
generated
output of decode: path or MuData.
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type.
max_per_label · default 200
most cells per cell type.
max_total · default 4000
most cells in total.
ilisi · default False
also compute the scIB iLISI (needs the optional packages scib and scanpy).
seed · default 0
seed of the cell sample.
Returns

One row per modality with pcc and scc (Pearson and Spearman correlation of the mean profiles), mmd and mmd_multiscale (on 50 principal components), knn_mixing and, on request, ilisi.

Example
python
mf.metrics.evaluate_generation("test.h5mu", "generated_profiles.h5mu")

functionmetrics.evaluate_perturbationmultiflow

evaluate_perturbation(real, predicted, *, cell_type, condition_key="cell_type", perturbation_key="perturbation", control_perturbation="control", min_cells=5, top_k=100, ilisi=False) -> DataFrame

The perturbation metrics of the paper for one held-out cell type. For every perturbation, the predicted cells are compared with the observed ones on the genes that respond most strongly in the observed data.

Parameters
real
observed raw RNA counts: path of an H5MU file, a MuData, or the RNA AnnData.
predicted
output of predict_perturbations: path or MuData.
cell_type
the held-out cell type.
condition_key · default "cell_type"
column of rna.obs with the cell type.
perturbation_key · default "perturbation"
column of rna.obs with the perturbation.
control_perturbation · default "control"
name of the unperturbed condition.
min_cells · default 5
perturbations with fewer observed or predicted cells are skipped.
top_k · default 100
number of genes with the largest absolute t statistic (perturbed against control) that are used.
ilisi · default False
also compute the scIB iLISI.
Returns

One row per perturbation with pcc_delta, delta_mse and mmd on the top genes, pcc_delta_all and delta_mse_all on all genes, the numbers of cells and the names of the top genes.

Example
python
mf.metrics.evaluate_perturbation("GSE274113_filtered.h5mu", "predicted.h5mu", cell_type="Pro-E")

functionmetrics.perturbation_metricsmultiflow

perturbation_metrics(real_control, real_perturbed, predicted, *, top_k=100, n_components=20, max_cells=2000, ilisi=False, seed=0) -> dict

The perturbation metrics for three RNA matrices on the log1p CP10k scale: observed control cells, observed perturbed cells and predicted cells of one cell type. The predicted and the observed change are both measured from the observed control mean.

Parameters
real_control
observed control cells × genes.
real_perturbed
observed perturbed cells × genes.
predicted
predicted cells × genes.
top_k · default 100
number of top genes.
n_components · default 20
principal components for MMD.
max_cells · default 2000

ilisi · default False

seed · default 0

functionmetrics.rank_genes_by_t_testmultiflow

rank_genes_by_t_test(group, reference) -> ndarray

Gene indices ordered by decreasing absolute Welch t statistic between two groups of cells. The statistic is the one of scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups(method="t-test") with a reference group.

functionmetrics.rbf_mmdmultiflow

rbf_mmd(real, generated, *, unbiased=True) -> float

Squared maximum mean discrepancy with one Gaussian kernel whose width is the median squared distance between all cells. unbiased=True leaves out each cell's distance to itself.

functionmetrics.multiscale_rbf_mmdmultiflow

multiscale_rbf_mmd(real, generated, *, kernel_mul=2.0, kernel_num=5) -> float

Squared MMD with a sum of five Gaussian kernels around the mean squared distance, the estimator of the scDiffusion-X evaluation.

functionmetrics.knn_mixingmultiflow

knn_mixing(real, generated, *, k=90) -> float

How evenly two sets of cells mix among each cell's k nearest neighbours: the inverse Simpson index of the two sources, rescaled to 0 (separate) to 1 (half and half) and averaged over cells. A dependency-free relative of iLISI.

functionmetrics.scib_ilisimultiflow

scib_ilisi(real, generated, *, n_neighbors=10, k0=90) -> float

The graph iLISI of scIB between two embeddings (0 = separate, 1 = mixed). Needs scib and scanpy: pip install "multiflow-omics[ilisi] @ git+https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow.git".

functionmetrics.pca_embeddingmultiflow

pca_embedding(real, generated, *, n_components=50, seed=0) -> tuple[ndarray, ndarray]

Principal-component scores of two sets of cells, fitted on both together.

functionmetrics.log1p_cp10kmultiflow

log1p_cp10k(counts) -> ndarray

log1p of counts scaled to 10,000 per cell, as a dense array; the same result as Scanpy's normalize_total(target_sum=1e4) followed by log1p.

Models#

classMultiFlowalias of CellStateFlowmultiflow

MultiFlow(rna_dim, atac_dim, hidden_dim=512, num_blocks=2, num_classes=None, cross_attention_dim=64)

Cell-type-conditioned paired RNA/ATAC vector field: two streams coupled by three bidirectional cross-attention modules (see Models). Calling the model returns the RNA and ATAC velocities.

Parameters
rna_dimint
width of the RNA latent state (128 in the paper).
atac_dimint
width of the ATAC latent state (128 in the paper).
hidden_dimint · default 512
width of each stream; also the size of each attention map.
num_blocksint · default 2
residual blocks before and after the middle block.
num_classesint | None · default None
number of cell types; None trains an unconditional model.
cross_attention_dimint · default 64
query, key and value width per hidden feature.
Returns

model(x_rna, x_atac, time, label=None) returns (v_rna, v_atac), each shaped like its input [batch, dim]. model.get_config() returns the dictionary used to rebuild it.

classMultiFlowPerturbationalias of PerturbationFlowmultiflow

MultiFlowPerturbation(rna_dim, atac_dim, context_matrix=None, *, num_contexts=None, context_dim=None, hidden_dim=512, num_blocks=2, cross_attention_dim=64, freeze_context=True, context_scale=1.0, num_perturbations=1, perturbation_scale=1.0)

Context- and perturbation-conditioned vector field with the same coupled streams. The condition is the layer-normalised sum of the time, context and perturbation embeddings. Perturbation index 0 is the control: its embedding is exactly zero and receives no gradient.

Parameters
context_matrixTensor [contexts, width] | None · default None
one row per cell context, e.g. the mean encoder state of each cell type. Its width must equal hidden_dim or half of it (then it is duplicated).
num_contexts, context_dimint | None · default None
build a zero context matrix of this shape when no matrix is given.
freeze_contextbool · default True
keep the context embedding fixed during training.
context_scalefloat · default 1.0
weight of the context embedding in the condition.
num_perturbationsint · default 1
number of perturbations including the control at index 0.
perturbation_scalefloat · default 1.0
weight of the perturbation embedding in the condition.
other arguments
as in MultiFlow.
Returns

model(x_rna, x_atac, time, label=context_index, pert_label=perturbation_index) returns (v_rna, v_atac).

classMultiFlowConcatalias of ConditionalConcatFlowmultiflow

MultiFlowConcat(rna_dim, atac_dim, hidden_dim=512, num_layers=8, num_classes=None, dropout=0.1)

The concatenation ablation of the benchmark: RNA and ATAC are concatenated and processed by one network. It uses the historical shared source (noise_mode="shared"), which requires equal RNA and ATAC widths. Kept for reproducibility; it is not the canonical MultiFlow architecture.

Parameters
num_layersint · default 8
depth of the network.
dropoutfloat · default 0.1
dropout rate.
other arguments
as in MultiFlow.

classBidirectionalCrossAttentionmultiflow

BidirectionalCrossAttention(channels, attention_dim=64)

One cross-flow module. Each modality is one token whose channels are its hidden features (shape [batch, 1, channels]). RNA features attend to ATAC features and the reverse, giving two channels × channels attention matrices; each stream receives a residual update. See Feature-level cross-attention.

Parameters
channelsint
hidden width of the streams.
attention_dimint · default 64
query, key and value width per feature.
Returns

module(rna, atac) returns the updated (rna, atac), same shapes.

functionbuild_modelmultiflow

build_model(config=None, /, **kwargs) -> nn.Module

Rebuild a model from a configuration dictionary such as model.get_config() or run.json["model_config"]. model_type selects the class: "cell_state" (default), "perturbation" or "concat"; the remaining keys are passed to its constructor. Keyword arguments override the dictionary.

Example
python
model = build_model({"model_type": "cell_state", "rna_dim": 128, "atac_dim": 128, "num_classes": 22})

Training#

functionfitmultiflow

fit(model, rna, atac, *, labels=None, perturbations=None, config=None, verbose=False) -> TrainingResult

Fit the vector field to paired latent states by flow matching: for every mini-batch, a joint Gaussian source and a uniform time are drawn and the model regresses the straight-line velocity; the loss is the sum of the RNA and ATAC mean squared errors.

Parameters
modelnn.Module
a MultiFlow model; its rna_dim and atac_dim must match the inputs.
rna, atacarray or Tensor [cells, dim]
paired latent states, rows in the same cell order.
labelsint array | None · default None
zero-based cell-type (or context) index per cell; required for a conditioned model.
perturbationsint array | None · default None
zero-based perturbation index per cell; 0 is the control.
configTrainingConfig | None · default None
training settings; defaults to TrainingConfig().
Returns

TrainingResult with the trained model on config.device.

Raises

ValueError if the inputs are not paired, do not match the model widths, or the labels are out of range.

dataclassTrainingConfigmultiflow

TrainingConfig(epochs=600, batch_size=512, learning_rate=1e-4, seed=0, device='cuda' if available else 'cpu', standardize=True, noise_mode='auto', reseed=True)

Frozen settings for fit. See Training for each field.

Fields and arguments
noise_modestr · default 'auto'
'auto' uses the source the model requires: joint Gaussian for MultiFlow, shared for the concat ablation. 'joint', 'independent' (the same distribution, historical name) and 'shared' must match the model.
standardizebool · default True
fit a LatentStandardizer on the training cells and train on standardised values.
reseedbool · default True
seed NumPy and PyTorch at the start of fit.

dataclassTrainingResultmultiflow

TrainingResult(model, optimizer, history=[], standardizer=None)

What fit returns: the trained model, the Adam optimizer, the per-epoch history (epoch, loss_rna, loss_atac, loss_total) and the fitted standardizer (None if standardize=False).

functionseed_everythingmultiflow

seed_everything(seed) -> None

Seed NumPy and PyTorch. Call it before building the model so that the initial weights are reproducible.

Sampling#

functionsample_paired_latentsmultiflow

sample_paired_latents(model, n, *, label=None, perturbation=None, steps=100, batch_size=512, device=None, seed=0, standardizer=None, rng_mode='joint') -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]

Generate paired latent states by integrating the vector field from the Gaussian source with the midpoint rule.

Parameters
modelnn.Module
a trained MultiFlow model.
nint
number of cells to generate.
labelint | Tensor | None · default None
cell-type (or context) index for all cells, or one index per cell.
perturbationint | Tensor | None · default None
perturbation index for the perturbation model; 0 is the control.
stepsint · default 100
midpoint ODE steps (paper: 100 for generation, 50 for perturbation).
batch_sizeint · default 512
cells integrated together.
devicestr | device | None · default None
where to sample; defaults to cuda if available, else cpu; the model is moved there.
seedint · default 0
seed of the source draws.
standardizerLatentStandardizer | None · default None
if given, the samples are returned on the original latent scale.
rng_mode'joint' | 'batch_invariant' | 'legacy_interleaved' · default 'joint'
how the source is drawn; see Random-number modes.
Returns

(rna, atac), tensors of shape [n, rna_dim] and [n, atac_dim].

Example
python
rna, atac = sample_paired_latents(model, 1000, label=3, steps=100,
                                  seed=0, standardizer=standardizer)

dataclassLatentStandardizermultiflow

LatentStandardizer(rna_mean, rna_std, atac_mean, atac_std)

Per-feature mean and standard deviation of the paired latent states, fitted on training cells.

Fields and arguments
LatentStandardizer.fit(rna, atac, epsilon=1e-6)classmethod
estimate the statistics.
transform(rna, atac)method
return standardised (rna, atac).
inverse_transform(rna, atac)method
undo the standardisation.

Autoencoder#

classMultimodalAutoencodermultiflow

MultimodalAutoencoder(n_genes, n_peaks, *, rna_dims=(512, 300, 128), atac_dims=(1024, 512, 128), norm=True, norm_type="batchnorm", dropout=0.0)

The paired RNA/ATAC autoencoder: one encoder and one decoder per modality, each a stack of linear layers with batch normalisation and ELU. A port of the multimodal autoencoder of scDiffusion-X with the same parameter names, so its checkpoints load without conversion. Methods: encode(rna, atac), decode_rna(z, library_size) (expected counts), sample_rna(z, library_size) (counts drawn from the negative binomial), decode_atac(z) (probabilities) and loss(rna, atac).

Parameters
n_genes
number of genes.
n_peaks
number of peaks.
rna_dims · default (512, 300, 128)
widths of the RNA encoder, ending with the latent width.
atac_dims · default (1024, 512, 128)
the same for ATAC.

functionfit_autoencodermultiflow

fit_autoencoder(rna, atac, *, config=None, verbose=True) -> AutoencoderResult

Train the autoencoder on matrices in memory (dense or sparse; batches are densified one at a time). train_autoencoder is the file-level version.

Parameters
rna
raw counts, cells × genes.
atac
binary accessibility, cells × peaks.
config · default None
an AutoencoderConfig: epochs 300, batch size 256, AdamW with learning rate 10−3 and weight decay 10−4, gradient clipping at 1, 10% of the cells for validation.

functionload_autoencodermultiflow

load_autoencoder(checkpoint, *, device="cpu") -> MultimodalAutoencoder

Load an autoencoder checkpoint in evaluation mode. Accepts checkpoints written by MultiFlow and Lightning checkpoints written by scDiffusion-X; the layer widths are read from the weights.
