Resources

Attention Explorer

An interactive page for the cross-attention of trained MultiFlow models. It shows the 512 × 512 attention map of the second cross-flow module and turns strong pairs of hidden elements into candidate peak–gene links, with gene tracks, GO terms and regulatory networks.

Open the Attention Explorer

What it shows#

  • Attention map. Rows are the 512 ATAC hidden elements (A0–A511) and columns the 512 RNA hidden elements (R0–R511). Each square is the cross-attention of one pair in CFM2 at flow time t = 0.90, averaged over cells. Click a square to select the pair and zoom in.
  • Peak–gene links. Gradient attribution gives each ATAC element a ranked list of peaks and each RNA element a ranked list of genes. A selected pair proposes a link wherever one of its peaks lies within 120 kb of the TSS of one of its genes; links are marked TSS, Promoter or by distance.
  • Gene track. The locus around a link, with reference tracks: H3K27ac for the OpenProblems cell types; ChIP-seq of the perturbed factor, GATA1 and TAL1, and GATA1 HiChIP loops for the Perturb-multiome contexts.
  • Elements and GO. The top genes and peaks of each element and the GO programs enriched among its genes.
  • Regulatory network. The strongest routes from peaks through ATAC and RNA elements to genes, for the current map.

Datasets#

Card Data Maps
Cell-state generation OpenProblems multiome, the cell-state model on real cells 22 cell types
Perturbation state Perturb-multiome, cells generated after a transcription-factor knockout 10 contexts
Control vs perturbation Perturb-multiome, the model on control and knockout cells; red pairs are stronger after the knockout 10 contexts

Contexts tagged held-out cell type were left out of training. Each map can be shared by copying the page address. A built-in tutorial (top right of the explorer) and a guided example walk through one finding step by step.

Reading the links The peak–gene links are candidates proposed by the model's attention. They are a starting point for follow-up with independent data such as ChIP-seq or chromatin contacts, not validated regulatory interactions.

How to cite#

If you use MultiFlow, please cite the software and the associated paper. The paper's DOI will be added here when it is available.

Software, version 0.2.0. https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow

  author  = {Wang, Haochen},

License#

MultiFlow is released under the MIT License, copyright © 2026 Haochen Wang.

Third-party components#

  • The paired residual and bidirectional cross-attention architecture was adapted from the multimodal backbone of scDiffusion-X (audited revision d60d928) and the MultiFlow research code. The scDiffusion-X checkout carries an MIT license at its root and a BSD 3-Clause license in its Python package; both notices are kept for the adapted parts.
  • The paired RNA/ATAC autoencoder (multiflow.autoencoder) is a port of the multimodal autoencoder of the same scDiffusion-X revision, in plain PyTorch and with unchanged parameter names. scDiffusion-X itself is not installed or imported.
  • The RNA VAE and the SCimilarity checkpoint-loading rules of the generation workflow were adapted from scDiffusion. Its hidden layers are initialised from the SCimilarity annotation model.
  • The tutorial datasets are distributed separately under their own terms (see Download) and are not part of the package.

References#

The methods, data and software that MultiFlow builds on:

  • Flow matching. Lipman, Y. et al. Flow matching for generative modeling. ICLR (2023). Liu, X., Gong, C. & Liu, Q. Flow straight and fast: learning to generate and transfer data with rectified flow. ICLR (2023).
  • Perturb-multiome data (GSE274113). Martin-Rufino, J. D. et al. Science 388, 52 (2025). Processed file: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.21986866.
  • OpenProblems multiome data. Luecken, M. D. et al. A sandbox for prediction and integration of DNA, RNA, and proteins in single cells. NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks (2021). Paired file prepared by scDiffusion-X: Figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.28582061.v3.
  • Encoders. The multimodal autoencoder of scDiffusion-X (revision d60d928); the RNA VAE of scDiffusion, initialised from the SCimilarity annotation model.
  • Data containers. Bredikhin, D., Kats, I. & Stegle, O. MUON: multimodal omics analysis framework. Genome Biol. 23, 42 (2022). Virshup, I. et al. anndata: access and store annotated data matrices. J. Open Source Softw. 9, 4371 (2024).

Release notes#

Version 0.2.0:

  • The package is self-contained: one pip install is all that both workflows need. The paired autoencoder is now part of the package; scDiffusion-X, scvi-tools, PyTorch Lightning and Scanpy are no longer required.
  • A Python API with one function per step (train_autoencoder, encode, train, generate, decode, predict_perturbations, ...); every function writes files and returns the path.
  • multiflow.metrics: the generation and perturbation metrics of the paper.
  • Two tutorial notebooks that reproduce both benchmarks from the raw data, with a quick mode on simulated data.
  • New commands multiflow paper train-autoencoder, multiflow paper train-rna-vae and multiflow data split; --autoencoder and --rna-vae replace the scDiffusion-X options of paper encode and paper decode.

Version 0.1.0:

  • Source-layout Python package for paired latent flow matching, with the cell-state, perturbation and concatenation models.
  • Feature-wise latent standardisation, midpoint ODE sampling, portable checkpoints and the multiflow command line.
  • The canonical source is one full-rank joint Gaussian over the concatenated RNA–ATAC latent space; the historical draw order remains available as rng_mode="legacy_interleaved".
  • Paired H5MU training and output contracts, with cell-type names kept in checkpoints.
  • Version-pinned, checksum-verified downloads of both tutorial datasets.
  • Leave-one-cell-type-out folds, the training-only mean shift and decoding.
  • Default sampling steps match the paper: 100 for cell-state generation and 50 for perturbation prediction.
